The sources disagree on whether Delhi's hottest days are getting hotter from January 1981 to December 2025.

NASA POWER (MERRA-2): clearly going down by 0.25 degC per decade (95% range -0.47 to -0.04).

ERA5 reanalysis via Open-Meteo archive: no clear change, 0.13 degC per decade (95% range -0.02 to 0.27).

NOAA NCEI GHCN-Daily: clearly going up by 0.25 degC per decade (95% range 0.11 to 0.38) (January 1981 to July 2025).

They can differ because NASA POWER and ERA5 use grid cells (about 50 km and 25 km wide), while GHCN-Daily uses a single weather station 3 km away with some missing months. Each monthly value is the hottest single day of that month, and months with fewer than 20 valid days are left empty. Land water storage across Punjab and Haryana is clearly going down, falling by 41.57 cm per decade, with a 95% range of -44.20 to -38.94 cm per decade, from April 2002 to June 2026. A change this steady would be very unlikely if nothing were really changing, well below the usual 0.05 line.

The data comes from NASA GSFC GRACE and GRACE-FO mascons (https://earth.gsfc.nasa.gov/geo/data/grace-mascons). GRACE satellites measure gravity over an area a few hundred kilometres across, not an exact spot. The measurement includes all land water together, so it cannot separate groundwater from soil moisture or surface water. It shows change relative to a baseline, not total water, and has missing months between mid-2017 and mid-2018.

Forecasts are not trends, so I cannot answer whether it will rain tomorrow. I only look at past observations to check for long-term changes over time, rather than predicting future daily weather. We do not produce weather forecasts.

For past data, the measurements available are air temperature, the hottest day of the month, precipitation, coastal sea level, and land water storage. These past records can show whether conditions in a specific place are clearly rising, falling, or showing no clear change.
